blocks.text: Hospital-acquired pneumonia (HAP) is pneumonia that develops 48 hours or more after hospital admission, which was not incubating at the time of admission.
It is an acute infection of the lung parenchyma acquired during hospitalisation and is associated with increased morbidity, mortality, length of hospital stay and healthcare costs.
HAP is particularly important because hospital-acquired organisms are more likely to demonstrate antimicrobial resistance compared with organisms responsible for community-acquired pneumonia.
A. Non-ventilator-associated HAP
Pneumonia developing at least 48 hours after hospital admission in a patient who is not receiving invasive mechanical ventilation.
B. Ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP)
Pneumonia developing more than 48 hours after endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation.
VAP is a distinct clinical category, although it shares several causative organisms and treatment principles with HAP.

blocks.text: Important: The organism responsible varies with the hospital, ICU, previous antimicrobial exposure and local resistance patterns. In Nigerian hospitals, local antibiograms and available microbiology should guide empirical treatment wherever possible.
HAP is suspected when a hospitalised patient develops a new pulmonary infiltrate accompanied by clinical evidence of infection.

items.text: New or progressive infiltrate on chest imaging.

blocks.text: No single finding confirms HAP.

blocks.text: Microbiology principle: Obtain appropriate respiratory and blood cultures before antibiotics when feasible, but do not delay urgent treatment in a patient with sepsis or severe pneumonia.
Unlike CAP, HAP does not have one universally accepted severity score equivalent to CURB-65.

content_groups.group_title: E. Risk factors for multidrug-resistant organisms

blocks.text: These are particularly important when selecting empirical antibiotics.

items.text: Previous IV antibiotic use within 90 days.
Previous colonisation or infection with MRSA.
Previous isolation of resistant Gram-negative organisms.
Hospitalisation for 5 days or more before onset of pneumonia.
Septic shock at the time of HAP.
Need for ventilatory support due to HAP.
High local prevalence of resistant hospital organisms.

blocks.text: High-yield distinction: HAP is not automatically multidrug-resistant simply because it occurs in hospital. Empirical broad-spectrum treatment should be based on individual risk factors and local resistance data.

Reduce complications, including empyema and lung abscess.

blocks.title: If HAP is associated with septic shock:

items.text: Administer appropriate broad-spectrum antibiotics immediately, ideally within one hour of recognition.
Consider an initial 30 mL/kg crystalloid resuscitation in sepsis-induced hypoperfusion or septic shock, with individualised reassessment.
Start noradrenaline when hypotension persists despite appropriate resuscitation.
Aim for an initial mean arterial pressure of approximately 65 mmHg, individualised to the patient.

blocks.text: Important distinction: HAP should not automatically be treated with meropenem, vancomycin or multiple broad-spectrum antibiotics. The objective is to provide adequate initial coverage without unnecessary antimicrobial exposure.

content_groups.group_title: A. Non-severe HAP with low risk of resistance

blocks.text: For patients who are clinically stable and have no significant risk factors for resistant organisms, narrower treatment may be appropriate.
Option 1: Amoxicillin/clavulanate (co-amoxiclav)

items.text: Duration: Initially 5 days, followed by clinical review.

blocks.text: This is a NICE-supported option for selected non-severe HAP without increased resistance risk.
Option 2: IV co-amoxiclav

items.text: Duration: Review after 48 hours and determine total duration according to response.

blocks.text: This is appropriate when IV treatment is required and local susceptibility supports its use.
Alternative: Other beta-lactams may be selected following local microbiology advice, particularly in patients with penicillin allergy.

content_groups.group_title: B. HAP with increased risk of resistant Gram-negative organisms

blocks.text: Common empirical approach
A broad-spectrum antipseudomonal beta-lactam is generally required.
Option 1: Piperacillin/tazobactam

items.text: Duration: Usually 7 days, subject to clinical response and microbiology.
Total daily dose: 13.5–18 g of combined product.

blocks.text: Option 2: Cefepime
Option 3: Meropenem
Meropenem is particularly useful when ESBL-producing organisms are suspected or confirmed and susceptibility supports its use.
Option 4: Ceftazidime
Ceftazidime has antipseudomonal activity but relatively weaker Gram-positive coverage.
Important: These regimens are alternatives, not drugs to administer together routinely. Selection must reflect the likely pathogen and hospital resistance data.

content_groups.group_title: C. When to use dual antipseudomonal coverage

blocks.title: Consider two antipseudomonal agents from different classes when there is:

items.text: Previous IV antibiotic use within 90 days.
High local resistance to the proposed monotherapy agent.
High mortality risk, particularly septic shock or ventilatory support due to HAP.
Structural lung disease such as bronchiectasis with risk of resistant Gram-negative infection.
Unknown local susceptibility in a high-risk ICU setting.

blocks.text: Possible combinations:
Option 1: Piperacillin/tazobactam + levofloxacin

items.text: Levofloxacin 750 mg IV or orally every 24 hours.

blocks.text: Option 2: Cefepime + levofloxacin

items.text: Levofloxacin 750 mg IV or orally every 24 hours.

blocks.text: Option 3: Meropenem + ciprofloxacin
These are examples of potential combinations, not universal prescriptions. They should be selected according to susceptibility data, renal function and individual risk.

Aminoglycosides such as amikacin or gentamicin may occasionally be considered as a second antipseudomonal agent, but their nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity make them less attractive. They should never be used as the sole antipseudomonal treatment for HAP.

content_groups.group_title: D. When to add MRSA coverage

items.text: There is previous MRSA colonisation or infection.
The patient has received IV antibiotics within the preceding 90 days.
Local MRSA prevalence is high or unknown.
The patient has severe HAP with septic shock.
The patient requires ventilatory support due to HAP.

blocks.text: Two preferred options are vancomycin and linezolid.
Option 1: Vancomycin

items.text: Loading dose: 20–25 mg/kg IV in critically ill adults.
Maintenance: Commonly 15–20 mg/kg IV every 8–12 hours initially.
Duration: Determined by clinical response and microbiology.

blocks.text: Target AUC/MIC for serious MRSA infection is generally 400–600, assuming an MIC of 1 mg/L.
Option 2: Linezolid

items.text: Duration: Usually 7 days for uncomplicated HAP, adjusted to response and complications.

blocks.text: Linezolid has excellent oral bioavailability, making IV-to-oral conversion possible when appropriate.
Important: Vancomycin and linezolid are alternatives for MRSA coverage. Do not routinely prescribe both together.

blocks.title: Paediatric HAP requires specialist assessment because:

items.text: Causative organisms differ by age and hospital setting.
Resistant organisms are common in paediatric intensive care.
Antibiotic doses depend on weight, age and renal maturation.

blocks.text: Do not directly apply adult HAP regimens to children.
Common paediatric reference doses

blocks.text: These are indicative reference regimens. Use age-specific paediatric formularies for exact dosing, especially in infants, children with renal dysfunction and ICU patients.

blocks.text: 1. Meropenem and valproate
Carbapenems can markedly reduce serum valproate concentrations, potentially precipitating breakthrough seizures.
Avoid the combination where possible. Increasing the valproate dose is generally not a reliable solution.
2. Linezolid and serotonergic medications
Linezolid has monoamine oxidase inhibitory activity.
Concurrent use with SSRIs, SNRIs, tramadol and other serotonergic agents can cause serotonin syndrome.
Review medication history and seek specialist advice when linezolid is required.
3. Vancomycin and aminoglycosides
Concurrent use increases the risk of nephrotoxicity.
Monitor renal function and avoid unnecessary combination therapy.
4. Aminoglycosides and loop diuretics
Concurrent use may increase ototoxicity.
5. Fluoroquinolones and QT-prolonging drugs
The risk of torsades de pointes increases when combined with other QT-prolonging medications or in the presence of hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia.
6. Fluoroquinolones and corticosteroids
The risk of tendon injury and rupture is increased.

subsections.subsection_title: 9. Adverse effects, serious complications and toxicity management

content_groups.group_title: B. Serious adverse effects and toxicity management

blocks.text: 1. Cefepime neurotoxicity
Particularly associated with renal impairment and drug accumulation.

items.text: Assess renal function and dose history.

blocks.text: 2. Carbapenem-associated seizures

items.text: Stop or change the causative antibiotic.
Treat seizures according to emergency protocols.

blocks.text: 3. Aminoglycoside toxicity

items.text: Stop or withhold the drug when toxicity is suspected.
Check renal function and serum drug levels.
Review other nephrotoxic or ototoxic medications.

blocks.text: There is no specific antidote for aminoglycoside toxicity.
4. Vancomycin nephrotoxicity

items.text: Adjust or discontinue treatment when indicated.

blocks.text: 5. Linezolid-associated myelosuppression

items.text: Review the need for continued treatment.
Consider discontinuation or alternative treatment if clinically significant cytopenias develop.
